extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of mythology and folklore
extracted.subtask_description: Methods, definitions, and evaluative principles for analysing myths, folk-tales, legends, and related folklore; includes comparative and reconstructive techniques and guidance on identifying origins, transformations, and cultural functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish myth, folk-tale, and legend (Gomme's definitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Myth: belongs to primitive stages of human thought and is the recognisable explanation of some natural phenomenon, forgotten object of human origin, or event of lasting influence. Folk-tale: a survival preserved amidst culture-surroundings of a more advanced stage dealing with events/ideas of primitive times in terms of unnamed human beings. Legend: belongs to an historical personage, locality, or event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these definitions to classify narratives; do not use the terms indiscriminately. The possession of three distinct terms is an asset only if definite meanings are agreed upon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess whether a folk-tale is a 'broken-down' myth
rubrics_metrics.description: Many folk-tales are merely 'broken-down' myths but not all; some were invented for amusement and are essentially fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek evidence (ritual traces, motifs, comparative parallels) before inferring mythic origin; avoid assuming all similar stories are derived from a single mythic source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Etiological criterion for myth
rubrics_metrics.description: Myths are recognisable explanations of natural phenomena, forgotten/unknown objects of human origin, or events of lasting influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a tale explains a natural phenomenon, cultural practice, or origins, treat it as a potential mythic account; use this as a diagnostic for mythic material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative method
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare instances of customs, tales, or rituals across cultures or within ethnological/political spheres to restore or understand original forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparison is valuable when comprehensive and technical; superficial similarity across cultures is not proof of common origin. Use comparisons cautiously—misapplied comparison can be valueless or misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complementary (reconstructive) process
rubrics_metrics.description: Build up or restore a ritual act or tale from a number of fragmentary examples scattered across regions or cultures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If analogous elements are found in different areas, infer missing features in a fragmented version. Restore a 'complete' example for comparison with similar survivals and living customs; this is especially useful when single isolated instances are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of philological analysis to separate folklore and mythology
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a distinction between tales susceptible to philological analysis and those which are not; this distinction is indispensable to scientific treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply linguistic and philological methods where possible to trace origins and relationships; be aware that terminology and meanings may shift over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer original/local evidence over recycled examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Where possible give examples from the author's personal notice rather than repeating well-worn citations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original observations avoid perpetuating errors and can show how universal tales are localized; favour first-hand or well-documented local material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for environmental/geographical determinants
rubrics_metrics.description: Beliefs about Heaven/Otherworld locations often reflect local geography (west/sea, mountain summits, sky among constellations, subterranean burial practices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting cosmological motifs, consider the community's environment (coastal, mountainous, plains) and mortuary practice, as these shape mythic geography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider mortuary practices in underworld beliefs
rubrics_metrics.description: Subterranean burial, cavern burials, and tomb practices influence conceptions of the Otherworld as an Underworld.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use archaeological and burial data to explain subterranean imagery and cavernous descriptions in literary/mythic accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trace socio-political explanations for deity status
rubrics_metrics.description: Lords of Hell or underworld gods may be gods of a conquered/subject race relegated by conquerors; political history can explain changes in divine status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate historical conquest and cultic policy (e.g., priestly policies) as factors in the elevation, demotion, or transformation of deities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify syncretism and religious transformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Spirits, local deities, or corn-spirits can be grafted onto existing gods or later morphed into saints and well-spirits during Christianization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for ritual continuities (wells, festivals), name-latinizations, and functional correspondences (e.g., corn-god → ruler of the dead) to detect syncretic processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise astronomical/astrological correspondences
rubrics_metrics.description: When gods are identified with stars or heavenly bodies, this association can explain why gods were conceived as dwelling in the sky and the linkage of Heaven with the sky.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine priest-astrologer traditions and astral iconography where present; such identifications alter cosmological placement of divinities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use material culture as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Objects like swords and cups yield information about the lives, habits, and beliefs of past peoples and can inform mythic interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat archaeological finds as evidentiary alongside texts and oral traditions; artefacts can corroborate or nuance literary/mythic reconstructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyse motif formulas and reduce to core elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Universal tales (e.g., musician entering the Underworld) can often be reduced to a least-common-denominator formula explaining variants (mythic aim versus folkloric aim).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distil recurring tale-types into their functional components (actor, quest, goal, outcome) to compare mythic vs folkloric purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish mythic function from folkloric adaptation
rubrics_metrics.description: A motif's function may shift: in myth it may explain death and restoration; in folklore it may become a romance or quest for faerie love.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the intended function (ritual/etiological vs entertainment/localization) when tracing the life-history of a motif.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of facile diffusionist explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Similar stories across cultures do not automatically prove Aryan or single-source origins; non-Aryan and independent origins are possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider parallel independent invention via shared human experiences and customs, and seek concrete cultural or historical links before asserting diffusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use taboo names and linguistic survivals as diagnostic traces
rubrics_metrics.description: Taboos around names (animals, saints, ministers, totemic names) and 'names of power' surviving in language can indicate totemic origins or ancient cultic practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document local naming taboos, euphemisms, and ritual periphrases; linguistic survivals may reveal pre-Christian or totemic layers in folklore.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trace localization and literary influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Well-known continental legends (e.g., Faust) may be adapted into local forms with added local color and superstition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map diffusion paths and local variants; identify which elements are imported and which are locally innovated to understand cultural adaptation.
